metaTitle: Best Heat Shrink Label Printers in 2026
metaDescription: Handheld printers that mark heat shrink tubing for wires and cables, compared on tube sizes, battery life, keyboards, apps and tape costs for electricians.
expertTake: The SUPVAN G15M Keyboard is the pick for most wiring work because it prints heat shrink tube, cable wraps and flags from a built-in keyboard and a month-long battery. The VolenGo E1000 is the value pick for an electrician who mainly marks single conductors. Skip this category if you only label cables by wrap and flag, since a standard laminated tape printer is cheaper to run.
introParagraphs: A heat shrink label printer prints text directly onto heat shrink tubing, so the identification slides over a conductor and shrinks tight with a heat gun. Unlike a wrap label, it cannot unwind or slide off, which is why panel builders and network installers use it for permanent wire marking.

The buying question is about tube sizes and workflow rather than print quality. Each printer feeds a limited range of tube diameters, and the tape cost per marker varies widely. Battery life, keyboard layout and app support decide how pleasant a day of marking wires will be.

products.name: SUPVAN G15M keyboard Bluetooth printer with heat shrink tube
products.description:
The G15M Keyboard supports eleven label types, including heat shrink tubes, cable wraps, cable flags, marking tags and continuous labels. A built-in keyboard lets you type a wire number straight onto the machine, while the Bluetooth app handles longer lists. The 1200 mAh battery is rechargeable and the 0.2 inch print margin wastes less tube than older designs.

The tradeoff is bulk compared with the Mini, which is the same engine without the keyboard. For a technician who types more than they import, the keyboard is worth the weight. Against the Brother PT-E310BT, the SUPVAN is cheaper to start but lacks Brother's long record of tape supply.

In ownership, heat shrink tape cassettes are the recurring cost. Keep spare cassettes in the case, and charge the battery before a long job, since running out of tube halfway through a rack is the classic way to lose an afternoon. Label the cassettes themselves with the tube size so you do not load the wrong one. Swab the print head if text streaks and store the printer away from heat guns, since a hot tool nearby can warp the cassette. On a long panel job, print the numbers in sequence and sleeve each wire as you go, so a missed number does not force you to trace a cable back through the loom.
products.bestFor: Wiring crews who type wire numbers on site.
pros: Eleven label types including heat shrink
cons: Cassettes are the main running cost

products.name: SUPVAN G15M Mini portable printer with heat shrink tube
products.description:
The G15M Mini is the pocket version of the G15M, with a built-in 1200 mAh battery the maker rates for up to three months of light use per charge. It supports heat shrink tubes, continuous labels, fixed-size labels and cable labels, and a 0.19 inch margin halves the waste of many older printers. It runs from the Bluetooth app only, so there is no keyboard to type on.

The tradeoff is that every label goes through a phone. On a job with a hundred wire numbers, the app's import saves time, but a dead phone means no labels. Compared with the G15M Keyboard, it is lighter and cheaper but less independent.

Ownership is about keeping the app and printer paired, and storing cassettes cool. The mini body is easy to lose in a toolbox, so keep it in a case. Because it can print fixed-size labels too, one machine can serve both heat shrink and general labeling. That flexibility is useful for a small shop that marks wires on Monday and labels storage bins on Tuesday, though the lack of a keyboard still means carrying a phone.
products.bestFor: Technicians who value a pocket printer and phone-based lists.
pros: Up to three months of battery per charge
Prints heat shrink and general labels
Pocket size fits a tool pouch
cons: No keyboard, needs a phone to print
Small body is easy to misplace

products.name: Brother PT-E310BT industrial label printer, Bluetooth, USB-C
products.description:
The PT-E310BT is a mid-size industrial label printer with Bluetooth and USB-C, quick application keys for cable wrap, cable flag and patch panel layouts, and storage for databases and templates. It prints Brother's laminated TZe tapes and takes the company's heat shrink HSe tubing, so it covers both flat and tube marking. USB-C charging and file import make it practical for panel work.

The tradeoff is cost. It is a pricier unit than the SUPVAN machines and uses Brother cassettes that cost more per marker than generic tape. Against the G15M Keyboard, it has stronger layout tools and an established supply chain but fewer label types in one body.

Ownership is easy because tape is widely sold. Keep HSe cassettes in their sleeves, update the app and wipe the head occasionally. For mixed jobs where you need laminated flags and heat shrink in the same day, this is the most flexible pick. The USB-C port also makes it easy to push templates from a laptop, which matters when a contract specifies a numbering scheme that you must follow label for label.
products.bestFor: Installers who mix laminated flags and heat shrink on the same job.
pros: Takes both TZe tape and HSe heat shrink
Quick keys for wrap, flag and patch panel
cons: Brother cassettes cost more per marker

products.name: VolenGo E1000 heat shrink wire label maker, 12 mm tapes

specList.label: Kit
specList.value: Heat shrink and flexible ID tapes

products.description:
The E1000 prints on 12 millimeter heat shrink tape with a 2 to 1 shrink ratio, plus flexible ID tapes for wrap labels. It offers three cable modes and one-touch shortcut keys for common layouts, and the kit includes two packs of tape. The maker lists a 2024 tape upgrade for print quality.

The tradeoff is fixed width. At 12 millimeters it fits mid-size conductors but not the smallest or the largest tubes. Compared with the SUPVAN G15M Mini, it has more keys but a less modern battery pitch, and its brand is newer than Brother.

Ownership centers on tape supply. Heat shrink needs a heat gun at the right distance and temperature, and over-shrinking can smear the print. Keep spare cassettes and clean the head regularly to avoid streaks across the text. For a home lab or a hobby panel build, the starter tapes in the box cover the first few dozen wires, which is often all a weekend project needs.
products.bestFor: Electricians marking single conductors at low cost.
pros: Starter tapes included in the kit
Three cable modes cover wrap and tube
cons: Fixed 12 mm width limits tube sizes
Newer brand with less tape history

products.name: Vixic DM170 Bluetooth heat shrink wire label maker, 320 g
products.description:
The DM170 weighs about 320 grams and uses a 1200 mAh rechargeable battery with USB-C charging. It connects through the Print Master app and detects the loaded tape automatically, which prevents layouts that do not match the cassette. It prints heat shrink wire labels and fits easily into a tool pouch.

The tradeoff is brand recognition and support. The app and tape ecosystem are newer than Brother's, so confirm tape availability before buying a stock. Against the SUPVAN G15M Mini, it offers a similar lightweight format with different software and supplies.

Ownership is simple: charge by USB-C, keep cassettes dry and update the app. Wipe the head when prints streak. A light body is comfortable on long jobs, but it also means less stable handling on a workbench. Pair it with a small stand or a cassette case so it does not slide while you cut tube, and keep a USB-C cable in the same pouch.
products.bestFor: Field technicians who want the lightest Bluetooth unit.
pros: Smart tape detection avoids layout errors
cons: Light body is less stable on a bench

buyingCriteria.explanation: Heat shrink tubing comes in many diameters, and each printer feeds a limited range. The VolenGo E1000 uses 12 millimeter tape with a 2 to 1 shrink ratio, while the Brother PT-E310BT accepts HSe tubing across several sizes. A tube that is too small cannot slide over a connector, and one that is too large will not grip. Check your wire gauges before buying. Measure the largest connector or lug the tube must pass over, then add a small margin, because a sleeve that will not slide on is wasted tape and a wasted label.

A 2 to 1 tube shrinks to half its diameter, which grips most conductors. Higher ratios such as 3 to 1 handle bigger connector heads. The E1000 uses 2 to 1, and the SUPVAN machines list heat shrink support without a stated ratio in the data. Match the ratio to the largest part the tube must pass over. A tube that shrinks to only half its diameter will not seal around a bulky crimp, so for ring terminals and large connectors look for a higher ratio or a larger tube.

A built-in keyboard, as on the SUPVAN G15M Keyboard, lets you type a wire number without a phone. App-only machines such as the Vixic DM170 and the G15M Mini need a device for every label. Apps help with long lists, but a dead phone stops work. Decide how much you import compared with how much you type. A crew that works from a printed schedule benefits from a keyboard, while a team that exports a spreadsheet from a design tool gains more from an app with bulk import.

A battery that lasts a shift matters in a panel room. The G15M Mini lists up to three months of light use per charge, the Keyboard version is rated near a month, and the DM170 charges by USB-C. USB-C is easy to top up from a power bank. Cheap units with proprietary chargers are a nuisance. Battery life figures come from the maker and assume light use, so a day of continuous printing will drain a cell far faster than the headline number suggests.

The printer is cheap and the cassettes are the real spend. Brother HSe cassettes are widely stocked but cost more per marker. Generic cassettes cost less but may disappear. Count the number of wires you mark per year and multiply by the cost per marker to find the true cost. Remember to include the waste from the leader at the start of each cassette, since a short sleeve at the end of a run is often unusable.

Cable wrap, flag, patch panel and punch-down layouts differ in orientation and repeat. The Brother PT-E310BT has quick keys for several layouts, and the E1000 has one-touch shortcuts. These save menu steps over dozens of labels. If you only mark heat shrink, fewer shortcuts matter. Network installers who label patch panels and faceplates gain the most from these keys, because the layout repeats across dozens of ports.

howWeEvaluated.title: Tube compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked which tube diameters and ratios each printer accepts. The E1000 is fixed at 12 mm with a 2:1 ratio, while the Brother accepts several HSe sizes. Wider range scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Workflow speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared keyboards, shortcuts and import options. The G15M Keyboard and PT-E310BT stood out, while app-only machines needed a phone. We weighed typical jobs of fifty wires.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery and portability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared weight and battery claims. The G15M Mini's three-month rating and the DM170's 320 g body earned credit. Heavier units lost points on long jobs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cassette supply
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at how easy it is to find replacement cassettes. Brother's supply is widest, while newer brands need checking. We favored machines that also print general labels.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cost of ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed printer price against cost per marker. Generic cassettes cost less, but supply risk offsets savings. The lineup spans the low-cost E1000 to the Brother.

cards.label: Keyboard models
cards.text: The SUPVAN G15M Keyboard and the VolenGo E1000 let you type wire numbers directly. They keep working when a phone is dead or the app changes, and suit crews that edit labels on site.

cards.label: App-only models
cards.text: The SUPVAN G15M Mini and the Vixic DM170 use Bluetooth apps with list import. They are lighter and cheaper, and they excel when a spreadsheet drives the job.

howToChoose.note: Pick a keyboard for field edits and an app for long imported lists.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A keyboard or fast import, tube sizes that match your conductors and a battery that lasts a shift. Patch panel and punch-down shortcuts help for network work.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The SUPVAN G15M Keyboard suits panel building, while the Brother PT-E310BT adds patch panel layouts and the widest tape supply.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You mark hundreds of wires monthly or mix tube and laminated labels. The Brother PT-E310BT and SUPVAN G15M Keyboard justify their cost in time and supply.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You mark wires occasionally. The VolenGo E1000 or Vixic DM170 handles light work at a much lower cost.

maintenance.why: Residue on the head streaks the text. Wipe it with isopropyl alcohol on a swab.
Heat can shrink or warp tube cassettes before use. Keep them in sleeves away from heat guns.
Lithium cells age when stored empty. Top up at least monthly.
Adhesive and plastic dust dull the blade and leave ragged cuts. Wipe it with alcohol.
Bluetooth pairing and tape detection depend on current software. Updates add cassette support.

faq.q: Is heat shrink better than wrap labels for wires?
faq.a: Heat shrink grips the conductor and cannot slide off, so it suits permanent wire marking. Wrap labels are faster and fit bundles. Many printers here, including the SUPVAN G15M, do both.

faq.q: How much should I budget for a heat shrink label printer?
faq.a: The printer itself is a small share of the cost. Cassettes are the recurring expense, and Brother HSe cassettes cost more per marker. Count your yearly wire marks to estimate spend.

faq.q: Do I need a heat gun?
faq.a: Yes. A heat gun or a hot-air tool shrinks the tube. Keep it at a moderate distance to avoid smearing the print, and let the tube cool before handling.

faq.q: What size tube should I buy?
faq.a: Choose a tube that slides over the largest part, such as a connector, and shrinks to grip the wire. A 2 to 1 ratio handles most cases, while 3 to 1 suits large connectors.

faq.q: Can these printers also make normal labels?
faq.a: The SUPVAN G15M models print fixed-size, continuous and cable labels, and the Brother PT-E310BT prints TZe tape. The E1000 prints flexible ID tapes. Check each model's media list.
The SUPVAN G15M Keyboard and the E1000 have keyboards. The G15M Mini and DM170 rely on apps. Keep a phone charged if you use app-driven units.
